gloss: To make a relationship, reputation, or position firm and lasting.
examples: A trade deal would *cement* ties between the two countries.
Her second album *cemented* her reputation as a songwriter.
The win has *cemented* their place at the top of the league.

gloss: To criticize someone formally and severely, usually by an official vote or statement.
examples: The board may *censure* its own chairman.
Two senators were *censured* for accepting the gifts.
The committee is *censuring* him for misusing public money.
contrast: Do not confuse *censure* (SEN-shur, to condemn formally) with *censor* (SEN-sur, to cut material out of a book or film).

gloss: To put something in the exact middle of a space.
examples: *Center* the heading at the top of the page.
He *centered* the vase on the table and stepped back.
The photo was not *centered* properly, so we printed it again.
contrast: American English spells it *center, centered, centering*; British English writes *centre, centred, centring*.

gloss: To bring control of something under a single authority or place.
examples: The reform will *centralize* hiring in one office.
They *centralized* all customer records on a single server.
Power has been steadily *centralized* in the capital.
contrast: British English writes *centralise*; American English uses *centralize*.

gloss: To fasten or hold something in place with a chain.
examples: Always *chain* your bike to the rack outside.
They *chained* the gate shut for the winter.
The dog was *chained* to a post in the yard all day.

gloss: To do something risky and hope that nothing goes wrong.
examples: The ice looks thin — I wouldn't *chance* it.
She *chanced* a quick look over her shoulder.
They are *chancing* a two-day drive in that old car.
contrast: The silent *-e* drops before *-ing*: *chance → chancing*, but stays in *chanced*.

gloss: To describe the nature of something, or to be a typical feature of it.
examples: How would you *characterize* their relationship?
He *characterized* the meeting as productive.
The season has been *characterized* by heavy rain.
contrast: British English writes *characterise*. The first syllable keeps its *r*: KER-uk-tuh-ryz.

gloss: To hire a plane, boat, or bus for your own private use.
examples: The team will *charter* a plane for the away game.
They *chartered* a bus to take everyone to the wedding.
We are *chartering* a fishing boat for the weekend.

gloss: To make someone humbler and more careful, usually after a failure or a rebuke.
examples: A loss like that should *chasten* any team.
The scandal *chastened* the whole industry.
He came back *chastened* and much quieter than before.
contrast: The *t* is silent: *chasten* is CHAY-suhn, like *hasten*.

gloss: To make something seem less valuable or less worthy of respect.
examples: Constant discounts *cheapen* the brand.
That remark *cheapened* an otherwise serious debate.
He felt *cheapened* by the whole experience.

gloss: To choose only the items that support your case and ignore the rest.
examples: Don't *cherry-pick* the numbers that suit your argument.
The report *cherry-picked* two good years and skipped the rest.
They are *cherry-picking* quotes from a two-hour interview.
contrast: Written with a hyphen in American English: *cherry-pick, cherry-picked, cherry-picking*.

gloss: To add chlorine to water in order to kill bacteria.
examples: The city *chlorinates* its drinking water year-round.
They *chlorinated* the pool before the season opened.
Heavily *chlorinated* water can irritate your eyes.

transitivity: both — transitive (*chomp a carrot*), intransitive (*chomp on gum*)
gloss: To chew something loudly and in big bites.
examples: The kids *chomp* through a box of cereal every week.
He *chomped* on an apple the whole way home.
The horse was *chomping* at the long grass by the fence.
contrast: *Chomping at the bit* is a fixed idiom meaning impatient to start.

gloss: To laugh out loud in a gleeful, snorting way.
examples: He *chortles* every single time he tells that story.
The audience *chortled* at the mayor's answer.
She was still *chortling* about it when we left.

gloss: To baptize a baby and give it a name, or to give a name to something new.
examples: They will *christen* the baby in June.
The mayor *christened* the new ferry with a bottle of champagne.
The hall has been *christened* after the school's founder.
contrast: The *t* is silent: *christen* is KRIS-uhn.

gloss: To record a series of events in the order in which they happened.
examples: The film *chronicles* one family's escape from the war.
She *chronicled* the strike in a series of blog posts.
Their rise has been *chronicled* in three separate books.

gloss: To throw something carelessly or casually.
examples: Just *chuck* it in the back of the truck.
He *chucked* the old mattress into the dumpster.
She was *chucking* snowballs at her brother all afternoon.

gloss: To laugh quietly to yourself.
examples: The kids *chuckle* every time the dog does that.
He *chuckled* and shook his head.
She was still *chuckling* about it an hour later.

gloss: To cut away the foreskin of a male, usually for religious or medical reasons.
examples: Some parents choose to *circumcise* their sons.
He was *circumcised* as an infant.
Hospitals are *circumcising* fewer newborns than they did in the 1980s.

gloss: To keep something within strict limits.
examples: The constitution *circumscribes* the president's war powers.
The court *circumscribed* the agency's authority last year.
Their freedom of movement was sharply *circumscribed*.

gloss: To find a way around a rule, obstacle, or difficulty.
examples: Some firms *circumvent* the tax by moving money abroad.
They *circumvented* the ban with a shell company.
The software stops users from *circumventing* the filter.

gloss: To bring a group or a situation to a more orderly and humane state.
examples: New rules should *civilize* the comment section.
Empires claimed they were *civilizing* the lands they took.
The debate was *civilized* by a firm moderator.
contrast: British English writes *civilise*; American English uses *civilize*.

gloss: To climb somewhere awkwardly, using both hands and feet.
examples: Kids *clamber* over those rocks all summer.
We *clambered* up the bank to the road.
He was *clambering* into the back seat when the bus pulled away.
contrast: Do not confuse *clamber* (to climb awkwardly) with *clamor* (to shout or demand loudly).

gloss: To demand something loudly and insistently.
examples: Fans *clamor* for a sequel every single year.
Residents *clamored* for the council to act.
Reporters were *clamoring* outside the courthouse.
contrast: You *clamor **for*** something. American English spells it *clamor, clamored, clamoring*; British English writes *clamour, clamoured, clamouring*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he clanged the bell*), intransitive (*the gate clanged shut*)
gloss: To make, or cause something to make, a loud ringing metallic noise.
examples: The bells *clang* on the hour, every hour.
The gate *clanged* shut behind us.
Somebody was *clanging* a pipe down in the basement.

transitivity: both — transitive (*she clattered the dishes into the sink*), intransitive (*hooves clattered on the stones*)
gloss: To make a loud rattling noise by knocking hard objects together.
examples: Hooves *clatter* on the cobblestones every morning.
A whole tray of glasses *clattered* to the floor.
The dishwasher has been *clattering* since breakfast.

transitivity: both — transitive (*the cat clawed the sofa*), intransitive (*claw at the door*)
gloss: To scratch, tear, or grab at something with claws or fingernails.
examples: Cats *claw* the furniture when they are bored.
She *clawed* her way back into the race.
The dog was *clawing* at the screen door to get in.

gloss: To clean something thoroughly, especially skin or a wound.
examples: *Cleanse* the cut before you put a bandage on it.
The nurse *cleansed* the wound with saline.
She has been *cleansing* her skin with the same soap for years.
contrast: *Cleanse* is KLENZ with the DRESS vowel, not the long *ee* of *clean*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*clench your fists*), intransitive (*his jaw clenched*)
gloss: To close your hand, teeth, or jaw tightly.
examples: He *clenches* his jaw whenever he is angry.
She *clenched* her fists and said nothing.
He was *clenching* the wheel so hard his knuckles went white.
contrast: Takes *-es* in the third person: *clench → clenches*.

gloss: To reach the most exciting or important point.
examples: The festival *climaxes* with a fireworks display.
The trial *climaxed* in a surprise confession.
The season was *climaxing* just as he got injured.
contrast: Takes *-es* in the third person: *climax → climaxes*. It *climaxes **in*** or ***with*** something.

transitivity: both — transitive (*clink glasses*), intransitive (*the ice clinked*)
gloss: To make, or cause, a light ringing sound by touching glass or metal together.
examples: We always *clink* glasses before the first sip.
They *clinked* their mugs and drank.
The bottles were *clinking* in the back of the car.

gloss: To hide or cover something up.
examples: Officials *cloak* the deal in technical language.
Fog *cloaked* the whole valley by morning.
The project has been *cloaked* in secrecy from the start.

gloss: To hit someone hard, or to beat or damage them badly.
examples: Storms like that *clobber* the coast every fall.
Our team got *clobbered* forty to three.
Rising rates are *clobbering* small businesses.

gloss: To make an exact copy of a living thing, a device, or a file.
examples: Scientists can now *clone* several kinds of animal.
Dolly the sheep was *cloned* in 1996.
He is *cloning* the whole repository onto a new laptop.

gloss: To thicken into a soft solid lump, as blood does.
examples: Blood normally *clots* within a few minutes.
The wound *clotted* on its own overnight.
Her blood was *clotting* too slowly, the doctor said.
contrast: The *t* doubles before an ending: *clot → clotted, clotting*.

gloss: To beat someone or something with a heavy stick.
examples: Hunters still *club* seals on some of those beaches.
He was *clubbed* over the head and robbed.
Police were filmed *clubbing* protesters outside the gate.
contrast: The *b* doubles before an ending: *club → clubbed, clubbing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*cluster the chairs by the window*), intransitive (*reporters clustered outside*)
gloss: To gather in a tight group, or to put things into one.
examples: Shops *cluster* around the train station.
Reporters *clustered* outside the front gate.
The new cases are *clustered* in three neighborhoods.

gloss: To fill a space untidily with too many things.
examples: Don't *clutter* the slide with text.
Boxes *cluttered* the hallway for weeks.
His desk is *cluttered* with old mail and receipts.

gloss: To come together and form a single group or whole.
examples: Small protests sometimes *coalesce* into a movement.
Support *coalesced* around a single candidate.
The story is still *coalescing* in her head.
contrast: Support *coalesces **around*** a person or idea.

gloss: To write a book, paper, or report together with someone else.
examples: The two scientists *coauthor* a paper almost every year.
She *coauthored* the study with her former student.
The bill was *coauthored* by members of both parties.
contrast: Often written with a hyphen, *co-author*; both spellings are standard in American English.

gloss: To tilt part of the body to one side, or to pull back the hammer of a gun.
examples: Dogs *cock* their heads when they hear a strange sound.
She *cocked* an eyebrow but said nothing.
He was *cocking* the rifle when the deer bolted.

gloss: To write rules or practices down as a formal, official system.
examples: Lawmakers want to *codify* the right in state law.
The agreement *codified* what had been an informal habit.
Those safety standards were *codified* in the 1970s.
contrast: The *-y* changes to *-ie-*: *codify → codifies, codified*, but *codifying* keeps the *y*.

gloss: To live together as a couple without being married.
examples: More couples *cohabit* now than a generation ago.
They *cohabited* for six years before the wedding.
She has been *cohabiting* with her partner since college.
contrast: One *t* in American English: *cohabited, cohabiting*. You *cohabit **with*** someone.

transitivity: both — transitive (*coil the hose*), intransitive (*the snake coiled*)
gloss: To wind something into a ring or spiral, or to take that shape.
examples: *Coil* the hose before you put it away.
The snake *coiled* around a low branch.
A long cable was *coiled* neatly by the door.

gloss: To invent a new word or phrase.
examples: Journalists *coin* new terms every election.
He *coined* the phrase in a 1998 essay.
The word was *coined* long before the internet existed.

gloss: To happen at the same time as something else, or to match it exactly.
examples: The two holidays sometimes *coincide*.
Her visit *coincided* with the first snow of the year.
The dates have *coincided* three years in a row.
contrast: One event *coincides **with*** another.

gloss: To gather information or pages together and put them in order.
examples: The office *collates* the results every Friday.
She *collated* the survey answers into one spreadsheet.
The copies have already been *collated* and stapled.

gloss: To cooperate secretly in order to cheat or deceive other people.
examples: Regulators asked whether the airlines *collude* on prices.
Two suppliers *colluded* to keep their bids high.
He denied ever *colluding* with anyone in the company.
contrast: You *collude **with*** someone ***on*** or ***in*** something.

gloss: To settle in a place and take control of it, or (of plants and animals) to spread into a new area.
examples: Bacteria *colonize* the gut in the first weeks of life.
Spain *colonized* the region in the sixteenth century.
The islands were *colonized* twice within a hundred years.
contrast: British English writes *colonise*; American English uses *colonize*.

gloss: To take something for your own use, especially by force or official authority.
examples: Troops sometimes *commandeer* private vehicles.
The police *commandeered* a taxi to follow the van.
Our meeting room has been *commandeered* by the sales team.

gloss: To do something to honor the memory of a person or an event.
examples: Each year they *commemorate* the fire with a moment of silence.
The stamp *commemorated* the first moon landing.
The city is *commemorating* the anniversary with a free concert.

gloss: To turn something into a business that makes money, often spoiling its original character.
examples: Startups race to *commercialize* the technology.
Critics say the holiday has been *commercialized* beyond recognition.
They are *commercializing* research that took decades to finish.
contrast: British English writes *commercialise*; American English uses *commercialize*.

gloss: To carry out something wrong or serious, or to set aside money, people, or time for a purpose.
examples: Most people who *commit* this offense never go to jail.
He *committed* the same error twice in one game.
The company has *committed* two million dollars to the project.
contrast: The *t* doubles before an ending: *commit → committed, committing* — but the noun *commitment* keeps a single *t*.

gloss: To press something firmly together so that it takes up less space.
examples: These machines *compact* the trash into solid blocks.
Heavy trucks *compacted* the soil along the path.
The snow had been *compacted* into a sheet of ice.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable, kuhm-PAKT; the noun and adjective *compact* (*a compact car*) are stressed on the first, KAHM-pakt.

gloss: To force someone to do something, or to make something unavoidable.
examples: A court can *compel* a witness to testify.
Bad weather *compelled* them to turn back.
He felt *compelled* to apologize in front of everyone.
contrast: The *l* doubles before an ending: *compel → compelled, compelling*.

gloss: To make a problem worse, or to add interest to a sum so that it grows on itself.
examples: Late fees only *compound* the debt.
Heavy rain *compounded* the traffic problems.
The interest is *compounded* monthly, not yearly.
contrast: The verb is kuhm-POWND; the noun *compound* (*a chemical compound*, *a walled compound*) is KAHM-pownd.

gloss: To be made up of a number of parts.
examples: Four small parties *comprise* the ruling coalition.
The old town *comprised* nothing but a church and a store.
Eight states, *comprising* a third of the population, opposed the plan.
contrast: The whole *comprises* the parts, never the other way round; careful writers avoid *is comprised of* and use *consists of* or *is composed of* instead.

gloss: To cheat someone out of money or trust by lying to them.
examples: Scammers *con* older people out of their savings every day.
He *conned* her into signing the papers.
She realized she had been *conned* only weeks later.
contrast: The *n* doubles before an ending: *con → conned, conning*.

gloss: To form a clear general idea of something, or to think about it in a particular way.
examples: It helps to *conceptualize* the problem as a network.
Early doctors *conceptualized* the disease as a punishment.
We are still *conceptualizing* the next version of the app.
contrast: British English writes *conceptualise*; American English uses *conceptualize*.

gloss: To affect or involve someone, or to make them worried.
examples: These rules *concern* everyone in the building.
The test results *concerned* her doctor.
Parents have been *concerned* about the new schedule.
contrast: You are *concerned **about*** a worry, but *concerned **with*** a subject you deal with.

gloss: To invent a story or excuse, or to put together a dish from whatever is at hand.
examples: He can *concoct* a meal out of almost nothing.
They *concocted* an alibi on the drive home.
She was *concocting* some sort of punch in the kitchen.

gloss: To agree with someone or with an opinion.
examples: Most experts *concur* on that point.
Two of the justices *concurred* but wrote separately.
Having *concurred* on the facts, the two sides still argued about the penalty.
contrast: The *r* doubles before an ending: *concur → concurred, concurring*. You *concur **with*** a person and *concur **on*** or ***in*** a point.

gloss: To injure someone's brain with a blow to the head.
examples: A hit like that can *concuss* a player even with a helmet on.
He *concussed* himself falling off a ladder.
Two of their forwards have been *concussed* this month.
contrast: Takes *-es* in the third person: *concuss → concusses*. The noun is *concussion*.

gloss: To treat someone as if you were better than they are, or to lower yourself to do something.
examples: Try not to *condescend* to the audience.
He finally *condescended* to explain it one more time.
Nobody likes being *condescended* to.
contrast: You *condescend **to*** someone. The participle *condescending* is used as an adjective: *a condescending tone*.

gloss: To treat two different things as if they were one and the same.
examples: People often *conflate* the two diseases.
The article *conflated* cost and value.
Those two terms are constantly being *conflated* in the press.
contrast: You *conflate* one thing ***with*** another.

gloss: To clash with something else, or to be in opposition to it.
examples: The two accounts *conflict* on almost every detail.
Her class schedule *conflicted* with the meeting.
We found *conflicting* reports about the time of the crash.
contrast: The verb is kuhn-FLIKT; the noun *conflict* (*an armed conflict*) is KAHN-flikt. One thing *conflicts **with*** another.

gloss: To confuse or surprise someone by defeating what they expected.
examples: The results *confound* everything we assumed.
The team *confounded* its critics and won the title.
Researchers worry that age is *confounding* the data.
